source.title: Steering MoE LLMs via Expert (De)Activation
source.authors: Mohsen Fayyaz; Ali Modarressi; Hanieh Deilamsalehy; Franck Dernoncourt; Ryan A. Rossi; Trung Bui; Hinrich Schutze; Nan-Yun Peng

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The safety benchmark results in Figure 3 are presented graphically; the paper also describes their overall pattern in text.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates GCG adversarial suffixes against safety-trained MoE models using safe-response rates, a direct test of the suffix-attack part of V4 on different models. It does not test the first-token mechanism.
record.gate_note: The paper tests inference-time expert routing and reports safety outcomes, including outcomes for jailbreak methods. It does not fine-tune on harmful or benign examples, measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, prefill compliant response tokens, change decoding, or test whether safety is carried by a small set of weights or ranks. The cited claim about safety being more than a few tokens deep is not tested here. Faithfulness results do not bear on the claim. Figure 3 is summarized under fits_no_version; its separate plotted condition values are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study's main result bears on V5 in a new setting, MoE LLMs. Deactivating a small, behaviour-linked set of experts degrades refusal, while randomly chosen or bottom-k experts of the same count do not. It also runs its own GCG suffix baseline, which bears weakly on V4: the suffixes were optimized for LLaMA-2-Chat and transferred, not optimized against these models. It does not test V1–V3, V6 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also say the router treats safety as a sparse subnetwork of experts. They argue that, like the few-tokens point of Qi et al., alignment must go deeper than a few expert pathways.
record.recipe_differences: The study changes expert routing at inference time rather than fine-tuning on examples, pre-filling response tokens, or measuring token-position KL. It also evaluates GCG as a jailbreak baseline.
record.method_sensitivity: Safety outcomes vary by model and jailbreak method; the reported safe-response rates for standalone jailbreaks differ substantially across models. Cross-lingual SteerMoE results also vary by language.

fits_no_version.finding: Inference-time routing toward safe experts raises safety by up to +20% with no over-refusal on the Harmless set.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Routing to safety-linked experts can strengthen refusal without training.

fits_no_version.finding: Experts detected on English pairs jailbreak the model in Italian and Thai as well.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-linked experts are shared across languages.

record.problems: Table 2 reports results on 50 AdvBench examples. The paper does not report uncertainty estimates for the safety results. Figure 3 is graphical, and the individual plotted values are not transcribed here. Safety is assessed using Llama-Guard-3-8B; benign compliance uses refusal-phrase matching, and fluency is judged by Gemma-3-27B-it.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 contains separate model-by-dataset safety rates for multiple steering conditions; these plotted values were not extracted individually, with the paper's textual aggregate summaries recorded in r44-r45. Faithfulness benchmark results were left out as unrelated to the claim.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis.
Prefilling, decoding changes, and target-optimized suffixes.
Dense models; weight-level or rank-level localization; pruning rather than routing.

missing.what: Per-model, per-benchmark safe rates under unsafe and safe steering (abstract: up to -41%).
Number of experts manipulated per model for unsafe steering (e.g. 100/4608 deactivated for GPT-OSS-120B; 480/6144 deactivated plus 5 activated for Qwen3), which sets how small the safety set is.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label on V4 is too strong: the GCG suffixes were transferred from LLaMA-2-Chat, not optimized on these targets. Table A.4's 0% for steering alone conflicts with Table 2's 90% for GPT-OSS-120B; the reason is unclear. The safety judge is Llama-Guard-3-8B, and no uncertainty is reported on n=50.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning or harmful-example count is tested.
No benign-data fine-tuning or change in harmful compliance after benign training is tested.
No per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models is measured.

Tests GCG adversarial suffixes as a jailbreak baseline, but not compliant-token prefilling, bypassing the first response tokens, decoding changes, or the proposed first-token mechanism. The study's expert-routing intervention and its combinations with FFA/AIM are different bypass mechanisms.
It steers expert routing, but does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test whether safety shallowness is caused by training data or objective.
Does not train safety to extend beyond early tokens or test whether such training holds up.

source_check.notes: The sole primary PDF's SHA-256 matches the manifest, and its extracted text exactly matches the supplied arXiv:2509.09660v2 snapshot dated 12 February 2026; all four required images and page 1 were inspected, with no missing or failed required images or version mismatch. Visual inspection resolves extraction layout; Table A.4's unspecified AIM condition and 0% versus Table 2's 90% remain source-internal disagreements, and the source also inconsistently names OLMoE checkpoints; weight-preserving expert routing does not establish a minimal individual-weight set.

Table A.3: GPT-OSS-120B AIM alone 100% in all three languages; combined rates 9.5%, 11.4%, 7.3%. Table A.2: GPT-OSS deactivates 100 experts; Phi activates 5 and deactivates 50. Table A.4: random and bottom-k selections 100%, selected steering 0%; AIM status unspecified.
